title: The Lava Lamp: Goes Great With Acid
summary: Josh and Chuck open with banter about a live show Josh is doing on existential risks and a Kansas City Chiefs preseason broadcast he missed. They then cover the history of the lava lamp: Edward Craven Walker, the Queen's Head pub egg-timer device invented by Alfred Dunnett, the Astro Lamp and Crestworth company, the science of wax and water densities, the 1960s psychedelic boom, the American licensing and TV placements, the 1980s-90s revival under Cressida Granger (who renamed the company Mathmos), and the lava lamp's use in random number generation at Cloudflare. They close with lava lamp safety tips, a mention of a fatal stove-heating incident, and listener mail correcting earlier episode on board breaking.
topics: lava lamp random number generation Cloudflare

segments.title: Opening banter and live show plug
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck chat about lava lamps they have owned, plug Josh's October 8 live show on existential risks at the Bell House, and talk about a missed Kansas City Chiefs preseason broadcast visit.

segments.title: Edward Craven Walker's early life and nudist films
segments.summary: Edward Craven Walker is introduced as a former RAF pilot who ran a travel business, then became an underwater nudist filmmaker after a trip to the South of France. His 1960 short Traveling Light ran for six months in London, and he later invested in a nudist camp.

segments.title: Origin of the lava lamp at the Queen's Head
segments.summary: In the mid-1950s Walker saw a cocktail shaker-like device at the Queen's Head pub that was actually an egg timer invented by Alfred Dunnett. Walker bought the patent from Dunnett's widow for under twenty pounds, improved the design, and created the Astro Lamp.

segments.title: Science of how lava lamps work
segments.summary: The hosts explain that lava lamps rely on two mutually insoluble liquids of similar density, water and paraffin wax, with heat from the bulb making the wax less dense so it rises, cools, and sinks. Fine balance of densities and slow mixing are needed to avoid an emulsion.

segments.title: Early marketing, Crestworth, and the 1960s psychedelic boom
segments.summary: Walker first marketed the lamp as a high-end bachelor pad furnishing, and department stores rejected it. He formed Crestworth to sell it himself. In the 1960s hippies in London adopted lava lamps for drug use, and sales took off, though Walker was uneasy about the drug association.

segments.title: American rights, TV placement, and sales peak
segments.summary: Two Chicago businessmen bought North American manufacturing rights and marketed the product as the Lava Lite. Lamps appeared on TV shows including Doctor Who, The Prisoner, and The Avengers; a claimed James Bond appearance could not be verified. Sales reached about seven million a year by the late sixties, then declined by the late 1980s.

segments.title: Cressida Granger's buyout and the revival
segments.summary: Cressida Granger, a 22-year-old antique dealer, noticed vintage lamps selling and bought into and eventually took over Crestworth. The acid revival, rave culture, and Austin Powers boosted sales, and she renamed the company Mathmos in 1992. Production stayed handmade in Britain, and Walker remained a consultant until his death.

segments.title: Pricing of authentic versus knockoff lamps
segments.summary: The hosts compare the price of handmade Mathmos lamps, around seventy-seven pounds, with cheaper knockoffs, and note the company's refusal to move production overseas.

segments.title: Lava lamp care tips and safety warnings
segments.summary: Tips include replacing the bottle after about 2,000 hours, keeping the room above about 60 degrees Fahrenheit or 15 Celsius, avoiding drafts and direct sun, running no more than eight hours at a time, and never heating a lamp on a stove. A 2004 death in Kent, Washington, was linked to a lamp heated on a stove, and a man drank lamp contents and suffered kidney failure.

segments.title: Lava lamps and random number generation at Cloudflare
segments.summary: Cloudflare uses a wall of about a hundred lava lamps monitored by a camera, with the pixel data converted into random numbers for internet security codes. The hosts also discuss how humans cannot generate truly random numbers.

segments.title: Rewards card number tidbit
segments.summary: The hosts describe a popular rewards-program phone number that many people enter, so it can work at stores across the country.

segments.title: Board breaking correction
segments.summary: Listener mail corrects the earlier board-breaking episode: the grain should run relative to how the board is supported, not relative to the hand, and force equals mass times acceleration, not velocity.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts thank listeners, invite them to follow social media, visit the website, or email the show.
